SBICs invest in small business What you can get Check your eligibility Find an investor SBICs invest in small businesses An SBIC is a privately owned company that’s licensed and regulated by the SBA. SBICs invest in small businesses in the form of debt and equity. The SBA doesn’t invest directly into small businesses, but it does provide funding to qualified SBICs with expertise in certain sectors or industries. Those SBICs then use their private funds, along with SBA-guaranteed funding, to invest in small businesses. What you can get SBICs invest in small businesses through debt, equity, or a combination of both. Debt is a loan an SBIC gives to a business, which the business must pay back, along with any interest. Equity is a share of ownership an SBIC gets in a business in exchange for providing funding. Sometimes, an SBIC invests in a business through both debt and equity. Such an investment includes both loans and shares of ownership. A typical SBIC investment is made over a 3-year period. Isotope R&D and Production (DOE IRP) The DOE Isotope Program (DOE IRP), and its predecessor organizations, has been at the forefront of the development and production of radioactive and stable isotopes that are used worldwide. The Program supplies isotopes and related services to the Nation under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 and has the sole authority within DOE to produce isotopes for sale and distribution. The DOE IRP produces critical radioactive and stable isotopes in short supply for the nation or that no domestic entity has the infrastructure or core competency to produce. The Program is typically the only, or one of few, global producers for these novel isotopes. pages.text: Itemized deductions, standard deduction | Internal Revenue Service Skip to main content Itemized deductions, standard deduction More In Help Interactive Tax Assistant Tools Report fraud Tax scams Identity theft Notices and letters Appeals Frequently asked questions Accessibility Contact your local IRS office Contact an international IRS office Tax topics Other languages Top Frequently Asked Questions for Itemized Deductions, Standard Deduction If I must deduct points over the life of my mortgage, and I have a 30-year mortgage, should I divide the points paid by 30 and enter that amount on Schedule A of Form 1040? Answer: No. While you must deduct the points over the life of the loan ratably (equally), you don't divide the points by 30 years. Instead, you divide the points by the number of payments scheduled over the term of the loan (360 monthly payments in the case of a 30-year mortgage) and deduct points each year according to the number of payments you made in that year (less than twelve payments in some cases). If the loan ends prematurely, for example, because you paid it off or refinanced with a different lender, then the remaining points are deductible in that year. Note: This does not apply to loans refinanced with the same lender. Any deductible points not included on Form 1098 (usually not included on the Form when refinancing) should be entered on Schedule A (Form 1040), Itemized Deductions , line 8c "Points not reported to you on Form 1098." Close j333-1145's Diary osm 极简画法 Posted by j333-1145 on 3 May 2026 in Chinese (China) (‪中文(中国大陆)‬) . 前言 这些随想是在去年年底写的，也许对其他 mapper 有启发，故发布。 以下经验会让画 osm 变得高效、美观、简洁，避免 无线细化 。 正文 osm 本质是抽象、简化的地图，所以画面元素要少、整洁。增加过多的元素会导致地图画面杂乱无章、不美观，而且后期维护也很繁琐。 例：一条公路的两旁有人行道，除非有物理隔离（比如栏杆），否则推荐在道路上加 sidewalk=both ，而不是把两旁的人行道都画出来 要提炼出对象特征，想出表达完整又简练的画面布局，同时不要出现渲染错误。 直线要直、圆形要园、方形要方、弧线要优雅大气。 线条不宜有过多节点，尽量把多余的、又不影响整体的节点删掉 道路、河流、森林等图画，宜大不宜小，宜长不宜短，宜整不宜碎 能不重叠就不重叠。如果一片区域（比如小区、医院、学校等），有明确的边界（比如围墙），最好先画完内部道路、建筑设施，最后再画上土地利用 area=yes 。否则就不要画。 一般使用 iD 编辑器最简单。若想画整齐的方形建筑物建议用 JOSM，并使用 building 插件。 标签方面，非必要不多加。 Discussion Comment from 真中あお on 3 July 2026 at 09:23 提醒自己地图是对现实的抽象，不追求无限细化，这是很有意义的方法论d(`･∀･)b Leave a comment Log in to leave a comment

pages.description: James Botham is accustomed to working away from the spotlight, but his performance could not be denied against New Zealand.
pages.text: James Botham: Wales' unlikely hero in historic win over New Zealand - BBC Sport Image source, Huw Evans Picture Agency Image caption, James Botham was man of the match in Wales' historic win over New Zealand By Gareth Rhys Owen BBC Sport Wales Published 16 November 2026 James Botham lay sprawled on the Principality Stadium turf, pain and exhaustion etched across his face. Whenever the whistle blew, the Wales flanker in the red scrum cap took an age to rise. Precious seconds to recover. Nobody counts tackles when the ball is dead. But when play resumed, he was everywhere. Tackling, scrambling, hitting the deck and springing back up. By the final whistle, Botham had helped Wales beat New Zealand for the first time in 73 years. He was man of the match. And as the celebrations began, the tears flowed. Quite an afternoon for a player accustomed to working away from the spotlight. Keeping a Botham out of the headlines was always going to be difficult. His grandfather, Lord Ian Botham , is one of Britain's great sporting celebrities. Outspoken, charismatic and capable of turning cricket matches almost single-handedly, he is box-office. James is different. His game is built on tackles, chasing, wrestling and relentless graft. Few positions in rugby are less glamorous than blind-side flanker. But on Saturday, Wales' number six was the star of the show. James Briones James Briones is the Acting Deputy Assistant Secretary, Grid Upgrades in the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE)'s Office of Electricity (OE), recognized for his leadership and deep expertise in enhancing the reliability and resilience of the nation’s energy systems. In this role, he leads strategic initiatives that strengthen U.S. energy security, affordability, and dominance through innovative investments and modernization, paving the way for a more reliable and resilient energy future. Prior to rejoining the DOE, James served at Amazon Web Services (AWS), where he led global Security Assurance Programs. James brings over a decade of experience from his previous tenure at DOE, where he led cybersecurity R&D efforts to protect critical energy infrastructure. He also spent nine years at the U.S. Air Force’s Space and Missile Systems Center, advancing national defense technologies. He holds degrees in electrical engineering, information systems management, and an MBA, and is certified as a CISSP and GIAC professional. Articles by James Briones

South Korea also says it deployed fighter jets, while Taiwan says it "responded" to Russian military aircraft detected in their respective air defence identification zones. These are unofficial buffer areas beyond territorial airspace where governments identify approaching aircraft for security purposes. Moscow has yet to comment. DeWitt characterized people of Japanese ancestry during World War II. He insisted that even those who had been born and raised as U.S. citizens nevertheless posed a threat because their Japanese “racial strains” were “undiluted.” Under the authority of President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s Executive Order 9066, DeWitt ordered the removal of all Japanese Americans from the West Coast in 1942. Allowed to take only what they could carry, they were imprisoned, without trial, in some of the most desolate places in the country. Today, the National Park Service preserves those sites so that visitors may learn their story. Jeffrey Novak Principal Deputy General Counsel Novak was appointed Principal Deputy General Counsel in May 2025 and served as Acting General Counsel until October 2025. He is an Honors College graduate of Ball State University and a graduate of the Indiana University School of Law. During law school, Novak worked as a law clerk for Bill Cummings, formerly the United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia. After graduating law school, he served a two-year clerkship with the late Charles R. Richey, United States District Judge for the District of Columbia, before joining McGuire Woods, where he was elected to partnership. Before joining the Department, he worked in a variety of roles at technology companies over the course of more than 20 years, including managing litigation, compliance, patent, and public policy functions, while also serving on the boards of the Northern Virginia Technology Council, the Internet Association, and the Virginia Early Childhood Foundation.

Jeffrey Williams Banner Color Light Text on a Dark Overlay (Default) Jeffrey Williams Jeff Williams serves as the Acting Deputy Chief Human Capital Officer for the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE). In this position, he is responsible for the full range of human capital services covering DOE's workforce of 13,000 Federal employees. Working with the Chief Human Capital Officer, he sets strategic direction and programmatic priorities for the human capital organization and provides leadership across a myriad of teams responsible for DOE workforce planning, advisory services, hiring, benefits, policy, employee and labor relations, executive resources management, talent management, engagement, human resources information technology, and accountability. He provides oversight to shared service centers supporting DOE Headquarters, national program offices, and power administrations. Jeff has over 30 years of Federal service and has been with the Department of Energy since 2009. Jeff has served in various senior leadership positions within Human Capital to include four Shared Service Centers (SSCs) and the Office of Business Operations. The company said its mains gas, mini bulk tank and cylinder tariffs would increase by 1p per kilowatt hour (kWh) for all domestic and commercial customers from 1 December 2026. It said the increase reflected higher wholesale gas and liquefied petroleum gas costs amid disruption to exports and shipping routes in the Middle East after the conflict with Iran. Chief executive Graeme Millar said: "We recognise that any price increase is unwelcome, particularly during winter." Close jfd553's Diary Mapping Icefields Parkway, Part 1: A two-year mapping journey Posted by jfd553 on 4 November 2026 in English . Last updated on 6 November 2026. I spent two years mapping the areas surrounding one of the most beautiful drives in the world. Each morning, I looked forward to discovering and mapping an area adjacent to a one I did the day before. This diary entry serves as an introduction to a series of texts covering the challenges I encountered and how I overcame them. Included below are a few snapshots taken in the field, which capture the majestic landscapes along the Icefields Parkway. I have also added a “before and after” map excerpt, as well as a short video, to illustrate how my work gradually took shape over time. The Place The Icefields Parkway (Highway 93N), in Alberta, owes its name to the spectacular icefields and glaciers that line the road. The parkway, which is a 232 km stretch of highway cutting through Banff and Jasper National Parks, attracts between 1.2 million and 2 million visitors per year. The parkway offers exceptional alpine landscape, with glaciers, rivers, turquoise lakes, and breathtaking mountain views directly from the roadside (Figure 1). Bates It was the fourth sinking of its long career, and this time the old wooden fishing boat lay submerged for nearly six months in brackish water and mud. When the authorities finally hauled it to the surface and towed it to Port Townsend, Washington, in June 2013, the Western Flyer looked like a ghost ship. Veils of seaweed hung from its rotting timbers, and it was encrusted with barnacles. The insides were full of mud. At the boatyard the wreck was valued at $0, but a purchaser from California, John Gregg, paid $1 million for it, or more precisely, for its mystique. In the spring of 1940, the boat was chartered for six weeks by the novelist John Steinbeck, who had published The Grapes of Wrath the previous year, earning national acclaim, sudden wealth and death threats from reactionaries outraged by the novel’s populist message. pages.text: Join Open Jam Sessions for an Insight Into London's Grassroots Music Scene | National Geographic TRAVEL Join Open Jam Sessions for an Insight Into London's Grassroots Music Scene Across the city, a growing crop of music-making events is nourishing the capital’s grassroots music scene — and helping to alleviate loneliness in the process. The Five Points Jam brings together more than 30 musicians for high-energy performances. Richard Mukuze By Sam Kemp Published November 18, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). The jazz saxophonist Stan Getz once said that the best music sounds “like a good conversation among friends”. Right now, some of the most interesting musical conversations in London are happening at its grassroots venues, where open jam sessions are giving musicians of all levels a platform to improvise, hone their craft and form new friendships. Participants may not know their fellow musicians, let alone the genre or dynamic, so there’s no choice but to embrace whatever the night brings. It’s about getting lost in music, together. New Zealand's Southern Alps are home to one of the world's rarest birds: the black stilt. Natasha Bazika By Natasha Bazika Published June 11, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Clouds move quickly across the Mackenzie Basin, dragging shadows over braided riverbeds and dry tussock plains that stretch towards New Zealand’s Southern Alps. One moment, the landscape is washed silver; the next, it disappears beneath a sweep of weather rolling over the mountains. I’m heading deeper into this high country on a window of borrowed time, crossing the 46,950-acre wilderness of Glenmore Station, a merino sheep, deer and cattle station. Hours earlier, the same storm front had grounded my helicopter flight to the country’s highest whisky bar — The Bad Decision, on a saddle above Glenmore Station — before it could leave the tarmac. Now, I’m racing a temporary clearing in the weather to find something far more elusive than a dram of mountain liquor: the black stilt, or kakī in Māori, one of the rarest birds on the planet. “The Mackenzie Basin has its own weather system,” says guide Ben Laffan, who’s taking me on Tekapo Adventures’ Black Stilt birding tour , a newly launched birdwatching experience, directing our four-wheel drive up a rough track. pages.text: Journey Into a Prehistoric Cave That Trapped and Entombed Animals for Millennia Skip to main content Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Photos courtesy of Dr. Susumu Tomiya and public domain Natural Trap Cave is a pit in northern Wyoming into which countless animals have fallen and met their untimely demise since the Pleistocene. Paleontologists today find the cave a treasure trove — a stunning record of the species that have long roamed the area. The mammalian fossils left behind shed light on the climate, food sources and migration patterns of these species from earlier eras. Careful excavation work over the years that has involved sifting for bones, extracting ancient DNA, and looking for prehistoric pollen has revealed not just the plants and animals that once populated this part of the world, but also the ecosystems and climates that governed it. It also has required some rather advanced rappelling skills. In this episode, host Ari Daniel speaks with vertebrate paleontologist Julie Meachen and Smithsonian contributing writer Michael Ray Taylor about what rappelling into Natural Trap Cave reveals about its contents and what it can tell us about Earth’s past. Juanes & Mon Laferte: Tiny Desk Concert May 23, 2018 5:00 AM ET Felix Contreras Credit: NPR Colombian pop star Juanes and Chilean singer Mon Laferte recently wrapped up a sold-out tour of the United States, which (lucky for us) included a stop at the Tiny Desk. Laferte began the concert solo with the torch song "Pa' Dónde Se Fue" (Where Did You Go?). She sang the break-up story with a smirk that belied the heartache hiding in her poignant lyrics. Then, after a short set break starring the Tiny Desk engineer Josh Rogosin, Juanes joined her to perform the duo's sultry single, "Amárrame" (Tie Me Up). It's rare to see Juanes in such an intimate setting. After almost two decades of performing solo, the Latin pop star is more of a stadium and arena kind of guy. It's a treat to hear his voice unencumbered by loud speakers or crowd noise, and to see his facial expressions as he sings lyrics that many of us know by heart. This marked a return to the intimacy that fueled his earliest days and that's still present in the personal lyrics that have sold millions of records. That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race. The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris. But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances. Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values".
